platforms.title: If Sinusitis Won't Clear, Check These Three Habits
platforms.meta_description: Yellow mucus and a nose that won't clear might trace back to three habits narrowing the sinus openings even further, according to ENT research.
platforms.body_html:
Yellow mucus and a nose that's stayed stubbornly blocked for days on end feels a lot like a cold that just refuses to quit no matter what you try. But when the sinus openings stay swollen or blocked, secretions pool inside and inflammation builds into sinusitis. Three surprisingly common everyday habits keep quietly feeding that ongoing blockage without you ever realizing it.

Three Habits That Keep the Sinus Openings Blocked

First is blowing your nose hard. Forcefully blowing both nostrils at once spikes the pressure inside your nose, which can actually push bacteria-laden mucus further into the sinuses instead of out. Second is using a decongestant nasal spray for more than three days straight. These sprays feel like instant relief at first, but continued use triggers a rebound effect — known as rhinitis medicamentosa — where the lining swells and blocks up even more once the medication wears off. Medical sources generally note this rebound sets in after roughly five to seven days of continued use.

Third is spending long stretches in dry indoor air. Dry air thickens mucus and slows the tiny hair-like cilia that normally sweep it along, so secretions inside the sinuses have a harder time draining out. Stack all three together, and that explains why nasal blockage and yellow discharge can drag on long after the original cold has actually passed.

What Actually Helps Sinus Drainage

First, blow one nostril at a time, gently rather than forcefully. Second, if you're using a decongestant spray, don't go past three consecutive days — if congestion is still an issue after that, switch to a saline spray instead of the medicated kind. Third, keep indoor humidity around 40 to 50 percent; even hanging a damp towel in the room helps if you don't have a humidifier. Drinking enough water also thins mucus overall, which lets it drain far more easily.

Holding a warm, damp cloth over your nose and sinuses for a few minutes at a time can help too. The warmth increases blood flow and calms the swelling in the lining, opening up a clearer path for secretions to drain. Breathing in warm steam during a shower for a few minutes has a similar effect, especially first thing in the morning when congestion often feels at its absolute worst before the day even properly begins.

If keeping up with all three feels like too much, start by thinking back to your worst recent day of congestion — how hard were you blowing your nose, and how many days had you been using that spray? If yellow mucus and blockage last more than ten days, or facial pain and fever show up alongside it, it's worth getting properly checked out rather than just assuming it's still simply a cold. Sleeping at night with your head propped up slightly on an extra pillow or two can genuinely also help quite a bit, since lying flat lets gravity pool secretions inside the sinuses, while a slight elevation makes drainage noticeably easier — definitely worth trying first if congestion consistently tends to feel worst right before bed each night.
